name: Gluten-free diet for bloat

lead: A gluten-free diet excludes the proteins in wheat, barley and rye. Among appearance-focused users it is tried to reduce bloating and facial puffiness and to look slimmer through the midsection and face.

For people with celiac disease, gluten triggers an immune reaction in the small intestine, and the diet is the accepted treatment. In non-celiac gluten sensitivity, bloating is a symptom, and a 2018 crossover study suggested fructans may contribute more than gluten. No study of facial appearance was found.

paras: Users swap bread, pasta and baked goods for gluten-free versions or naturally gluten-free foods such as rice, potatoes, meat, vegetables and fruit, and judge the change over a few weeks. Physicians generally advise testing for celiac disease before starting, since the diet can affect test accuracy.

Nutritional gaps are possible, including iron, B vitamins, folate, calcium and fiber, especially when processed gluten-free substitutes replace whole foods. Going gluten-free before testing can mask celiac disease.

angle.text: Users drop gluten hoping for less gut bloating and a slimmer midsection and face. The diet is the accepted treatment for celiac disease, and no studies were found on facial puffiness in people without gluten-related conditions.

lead: A gluten-free diet excludes gluten, the group of proteins in wheat, barley, rye and related grains. Lifelong adherence is the only medically accepted treatment for celiac disease.[1]

Beyond celiac disease, some people follow it for non-celiac gluten sensitivity, a condition described as controversial with unclear causes and an estimated prevalence of 0.5 to 13 percent.[1] Since the early 21st century, the diet has also become popular as a lifestyle choice, including among athletes.[1]
In appearance-focused communities, gluten elimination is proposed to reduce bloating and facial puffiness. No published studies on facial puffiness were found in the sources reviewed.

paras: Bloating is described as a common gastrointestinal symptom in non-celiac gluten sensitivity. A 2018 crossover study of 59 people found bloating was borderline significantly higher after fructans than after gluten (P=0.049), and the authors concluded fructans may be the more likely cause; experts have suggested a low-FODMAP diet over a gluten-free diet for bloating.[1]

A 2013 placebo-controlled study in IBS patients found no difference between gluten and placebo, although the study had design limitations, and a 2015 trial reported that purified gluten triggered symptoms in people with self-reported sensitivity, without clarifying whether gluten or other cereal proteins were responsible.[1]
No studies found of gluten-free diets for facial puffiness or facial appearance.

Reported risks include nutritional gaps in iron, B vitamins, folate, calcium and fiber, particularly when processed gluten-free substitutes replace whole foods; many such products are less fortified and higher in fat, sugar or carbohydrates. Cross-contamination is also described, with one study finding 32 percent of restaurant foods labeled gluten-free exceeded 20 ppm.[1]
The medical consensus described is to consult a physician before going gluten-free so that celiac disease can be tested accurately.[1]
